title: With two overloaded methods — one taking `Object`, one taking `String` — which is invoked when you pass `null`, and why (most-specific rule, and when it becomes ambiguous)?
shortTitle: With overloaded methods taking Object and String, which is called for null?

s1_definition.profdef: When you call an overloaded method with a null literal and there are overloads taking Object and String, the compiler selects the String overload because of the most-specific-type rule: among all applicable overloads, Java picks the one whose parameter type is most specific, and String is more specific than Object since every String is an Object but not vice versa. The selection happens at compile time based on types, not at runtime. It becomes ambiguous and fails to compile only when two or more candidate types are equally specific with no single most-specific choice, such as overloads taking String and Integer, because null fits both and neither is more specific than the other.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine two counters, a general enquiry counter that accepts any request and a specialist account counter that accepts only account requests. If you hand in a blank slip, which is null, the bank sends you to the most specialised counter that can still accept it, which is the account counter, because a more specialised desk is preferred when it applies. But if there were two equally specialised counters, say one only for account slips and one only for loan slips, and you hand in a blank slip that could go to either, the staff cannot decide and refuse to route it, which is the ambiguity error.
s1_definition.oneliner: Passing null picks the most specific applicable overload, so String wins over Object, but when two candidates are equally specific the call is ambiguous and does not compile.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When you call an overloaded method with a null literal and there are overloads taking Object and String, the compiler selects the String overload because of the most-specific-type rule: among all applicable overloads, Java picks the one whose parameter type is most specific, and String is more specific than Object since every String is an Object but not vice versa. The selection happens at compile time based on types, not at runtime. It becomes ambiguous and fails to compile only when two or more candidate types are equally specific with no single most-specific choice, such as overloads taking String and Integer, because null fits both and neither is more specific than the other.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine two counters, a general enquiry counter that accepts any request and a specialist account counter that accepts only account requests. If you hand in a blank slip, which is null, the bank sends you to the most specialised counter that can still accept it, which is the account counter, because a more specialised desk is preferred when it applies. But if there were two equally specialised counters, say one only for account slips and one only for loan slips, and you hand in a blank slip that could go to either, the staff cannot decide and refuse to route it, which is the ambiguity error.

**One line to remember:** Passing null picks the most specific applicable overload, so String wins over Object, but when two candidates are equally specific the call is ambiguous and does not compile.

sections.s2_technical:
Overload resolution happens at compile time using the static types of the arguments. The null literal has no type of its own, but it is assignable to every reference type, so every overload with a reference parameter is applicable. Among applicable overloads, Java applies the most-specific rule: an overload is more specific than another if its parameter type could be passed to the other overload, meaning it is a subtype. String is a subtype of Object, so String is more specific, and the String overload is chosen for a null argument.

```java
void handle(Object o) { /* general */ }
void handle(String s) { /* specific */ }
handle(null); // calls handle(String) — String is most specific
```

If you want the Object overload with a null, you must cast the null to guide resolution:

```java
handle((Object) null); // now the static type is Object → calls handle(Object)
```

The ambiguous case arises when there is no single most-specific type. Consider overloads taking String and Integer. Both are applicable to null, but neither String nor Integer is a subtype of the other, so neither is more specific, and the compiler reports a reference-to-method-is-ambiguous error:

```java
void process(String s) { }
void process(Integer i) { }
process(null); // COMPILE ERROR — ambiguous, no most-specific type
```

To resolve that, you cast null to the intended type, such as process with null cast to String.

A senior point is that this is a compile-time decision tied to static types, which is why it is sometimes counterintuitive: the runtime object is irrelevant because for null there is no object. Another senior point is that relying on overload resolution with null is fragile and hurts readability, so in banking APIs it is better to avoid designing overloads that differ only by reference type when callers might pass null, or to provide clearly named methods instead, and when a null must be routed to a specific overload, an explicit cast documents the intent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A logging helper had overloads for Object and String, and a null argument unexpectedly went to the String overload, which the team explained with the most-specific rule. This is exactly the Object-versus-String resolution.

Problem 2 — Another helper had overloads for String and Integer, and passing null failed to compile, which the team fixed with a cast. This is exactly the ambiguity case.

The code defines an `AuditLogger` with Object and String overloads and a `Router` with String and Integer overloads, and an `OverloadNullDemo` main class that shows the specific choice, the cast to Object, and the cast needed to resolve ambiguity.

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are null arguments passed to overloaded methods, with and without casts.

Step 1: Calling record with a bare null makes both the Object and String overloads applicable, because null fits any reference type. The compiler applies the most-specific rule and selects the String overload, so the result is the string-tagged output.

Step 2: Calling record with null cast to Object gives the argument a static type of Object, so only the Object overload is the exact match for that type, and the compiler selects the Object overload, producing the object-tagged output.

Step 3: Calling route with a bare null would make both the String and Integer overloads applicable, but neither type is more specific than the other, so the compiler cannot choose and the call does not compile, which is why it is left commented.

Step 4: Calling route with null cast to String fixes the static type to String, so the String overload is chosen, producing the string-route output.

Step 5: Calling route with null cast to Integer fixes the static type to Integer, so the Integer overload is chosen, producing the integer-route output, which shows that a cast is the explicit way to resolve ambiguity.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: record(null) → STRING:null
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: record((Object) null) → OBJECT:null
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: route((String) null) → STRING-ROUTE:null
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: route((Integer) null) → INTEGER-ROUTE:null
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  record(null)
    │ applicable: record(Object), record(String)
    │ most-specific: String ⊂ Object
    ▼
  record(String) → "STRING:null"

  record((Object) null)
    │ static type = Object → only Object overload matches that type
    ▼
  record(Object) → "OBJECT:null"

  route(null)
    │ applicable: route(String), route(Integer)
    │ neither more specific → AMBIGUOUS → COMPILE ERROR
    │
    ├─ route((String) null)  → "STRING-ROUTE:null"
    └─ route((Integer) null) → "INTEGER-ROUTE:null"
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Overload Resolution at Compile Time ═══

  ┌────────┐  source  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Dev    │─────────→│ javac (compiler)  │  picks overload by STATIC types
  └────────┘          └───────┬──────────┘
                              │ most-specific or ambiguous error
                              ▼
                   bytecode binds the chosen method (runtime object irrelevant)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Most-Specific Rule & Ambiguity ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  I: prefer clearly named methods over null-ambiguous ones│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │        AuditLogger         │   │          Router            │
  │  + record(Object)          │   │  + route(String)           │
  │  + record(String)          │   │  + route(Integer)          │
  │  (String most specific)    │   │  (no most-specific → ambig)│
  └───────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────┘

  Rules (in sentences):
    null applicable to all reference overloads
    most specific (subtype) chosen when one exists → String over Object
    no single most-specific → compile error → cast null to pick

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. record(null)          → record(String)
  2. record((Object)null)  → record(Object)
  3. route(null)           → COMPILE ERROR (ambiguous)
  4. route((String)null)   → route(String)
  5. route((Integer)null)  → route(Integer)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When I call an overloaded method with a null literal and the overloads take Object and String, the String overload is chosen. The reason is the most-specific-type rule in overload resolution. The null literal has no type of its own but is assignable to every reference type, so both overloads are applicable, and among applicable overloads Java picks the most specific one. String is a subtype of Object, so String is more specific, and it wins. The key point is that this is decided entirely at compile time from static types, because for null there is no runtime object to consult.

If I actually want the Object overload with a null, I cast the null to Object, which fixes the argument's static type to Object and directs the compiler to the general overload. That cast is the explicit, readable way to guide resolution.

The call becomes ambiguous only when there is no single most-specific type among the applicable overloads. The classic example is overloads taking String and Integer. Both are applicable to null, but neither is a subtype of the other, so neither is more specific, and the compiler reports a reference-to-method-is-ambiguous error and refuses to compile. I resolve that the same way, by casting null to the intended type, such as casting to String or to Integer.

The senior lesson I draw from this is that depending on overload resolution with null is fragile and often surprising, precisely because the runtime object is irrelevant and the choice hinges on static types. In banking APIs I prefer not to design overloads that differ only by reference type when callers might pass null, and I favour clearly named methods instead, so there is no guessing. When a null genuinely must be routed to a specific overload, I use an explicit cast to document the intent. So my complete answer is that null selects the most specific overload, which means String over Object, and when two candidates are equally specific the call is ambiguous and must be disambiguated with a cast.

---

keyPoints: Most specific type wins — String is more specific than Object
null passed to method(Object) and method(String): String version called
If two equally specific overloads match (String, Integer): ambiguous, compile error
Compiler resolves overloading at compile time based on argument types
